newsitem.title: BELARUS: Thousands protest against Belarus president.
newsitem.headline: Thousands protest against Belarus president.

text.p: About 10,000 people defied a ban on marches in Belarus to protest on Saturday against hardline President Alexander Lukashenko and to mark the republic's Constitution Day.
"Long live Belarus!" they shouted, showing their opposition to plans for a union with Russia which President Boris Yeltsin said on Friday could eventually lead to a merger.
They passed a resolution calling for new elections to the parliament formed after Lukashenko won a controversial constitutional referendum last November on expanding his powers.
It also called for opposition forces to consider trying to push through early presidential elections.
"Fascism! Lukashism!" protesters chanted after police blocked them from proceeding down Minsk's central avenue, where Lukashenko's residence is situated.
Marches have been officially banned and police with riot gear and truncheons funnelled the crowds down side-streets.
Police used truncheons to break up a rally of up to 2,000 young activists on Friday, arresting about 100 people, including two Americans, two Germans and several journalists.

Protesters rallied on Saturday near the Palace of Sports where opposition politicians denounced Lukashenko's amended version of the former Soviet republic's constitution. The original was written four years ago.
The Popular Front, the most active opposition group, said seven protesters were arrested. State television later said 15 people were detained.
Yuri Khodyko, a Popular Front leader, began a hunger strike in the prison where he has been held since his arrest in a late-night police raid on Thursday, Interfax news agency said.
Khodyka's wife said the 53-year-old academic was protesting at being sentenced to five days for resisting arrest. Last April he staged a three-week hunger strike, also while in detention.
The referendum, widely discredited since Lukashenko ignored the constitutional court, parliament and the constitution itself to push it through, gave him wide authority over all branches of power.

It also allowed him to recommence his five-year term, giving him a total of 7-1/2 years at the helm of a state whose identity is intimately tied up with Moscow after centuries of Russian and Soviet rule.

Lukashenko praised his constitution as a "guarantor of domestic political stability" in an address in official newspapers. "The updated constitution created a foundation for fulfilling the individual's rights and freedom," it said.
But Semyon Sharetsky, speaker of the old parliament who led attempts to stop the November vote, told the rally: "Under cover of the so-called referendum, a coup d'etat has taken place in Belarus.
"Its organiser, spiritual leader and manager was Alexander Lukashenko, who brutally violated the old constitution."
Youngsters ripped up official Belarussian flags which had been put up for the holiday. Lukashenko revived the Soviet-era flag in place of the red-and-white one adopted on independence.
Earlier this month he banned the display of post-independence symbols as part of a crackdown on opposition forces.
Most of the republic's 10 million people apparently back the president but he is opposed by a loose union of liberals, nationalists, intellectuals and students mostly concentrated in Minsk.
Some 60 deputies who refused to join the new parliament met on Friday night to call on the outside world not to recognise Lukashenko's new constitution.
They were joined by the German ambassador, the Italian charge d'affaires and British and Russian embassy officials.
The United States said on Friday it had downgraded its relationship with Belarus because of what it called a "serious turn for the worse" in the human rights situation.
